label: GPT-6.1 Sol
output:
Kelechi,

You said if I was serious, I should put it in writing. So here we are. A proper letter, sent through the post, because apparently nine years in quantity surveying has turned you into somebody who requires formal correspondence before he can consider a suggestion from his friend. I hope you are reading this on the train as promised. Don’t leave it beside a Metro.

I am serious. I think you should consider teaching maths.

Before you start, I did not say resign tomorrow. Please don’t arrive at my house with a cardboard box and tell me I have ruined your life. I am asking you to come with me to the training partnership’s open evening in Lewisham on **Thursday 19 November, at 6pm**. Listen, ask questions, see what you think. You are not signing your life away. You can even fold your arms throughout, if that will help you feel independent.

At my birthday, when you started on the subject of that job again, I was teasing you, but I wasn’t only teasing. You have been at that firm for nine years. Every time we talk about work, it is the same spreadsheet, the same costings, the same feeling that you have already lived the following Tuesday. I know a birthday party is not the place for a full career consultation, especially when other people are trying to hear the music, but I heard you.

And I keep thinking about what you said on your last birthday: “I just want to do something that matters before 40.”

I’m not quoting that to trap you. Friends should be allowed to say things on their birthdays without somebody producing minutes later. But I don’t think you were joking.

I have known you since Unilag. Long before this firm in Croydon got hold of you, you were the person tutoring half our hostel in Moremi before exams. You got your A in further maths, yes, but being good at maths was only part of it. Plenty of people can get the answer and then look personally offended when somebody else cannot. You would sit there, find out where the person had got lost, and explain it another way. You never made anybody feel stupid for needing that second explanation.

That is what I remember. Not just that you knew it, but that people could ask you.

And you are still doing it. At Christmas, you taught my nephew fractions using portions of jollof rice on plates. The boy still talks about it. You were trying to help him understand something, and you found a way in through what was in front of you. Also, I noticed you made sure none of the teaching materials went to waste afterwards. Very committed educator.

I am not saying one successful encounter with fractions means you are ready for a Year 9 classroom. My nephew was not simultaneously asking to go to the toilet, arguing about a ruler and insisting that fractions would never be useful because he was going to become a footballer. There is training for a reason. But you have patience, you are funny, and you can explain something without turning it into a demonstration of how clever you are. Those are good things to bring into a school.

Let me tell you about Damola.

He is in Year 11. Last month, after three weeks of struggling with simultaneous equations, he finally got it. He looked at his work, looked at me and shouted, “Is that all??” As if I had deliberately been hiding the simple version from him for three weeks. The whole class clapped.

You would have laughed. I did. But I was also so pleased for him I could barely move on with the lesson. He had spent all that time expecting not to understand, and then he could do it himself.

I don’t get a moment like that every day. Some days the most exciting thing that happens is that the printer works. But I think you would enjoy helping a child get to that point. I think you would be good at staying with them through the three weeks before it, too.

Now, because you know me and you will detect nonsense immediately, let me give you the rest.

Teaching is hard. Marking is endless. Behaviour some days is proper wahala. You can prepare a lesson carefully and still spend an unreasonable amount of it dealing with something you could not possibly have planned for. There are days when you are tired before you have even started teaching, and still you have to stand there and be patient, clear and fair.

When I started in 2019, I cried in the car park twice in my first term. Twice that I am admitting to in a document you can keep.

I am telling you because I won’t sell you the nice classroom story and hide the car park. It got better. I learned, I got help, and things that used to throw me became things I knew how to handle. But I still have difficult days. You should speak to people at the open evening about those days, not only about the days they put in the prospectus.

You should ask hard questions about money as well. The route I have in mind is the salaried one: you get paid while you train, it lasts a year, and it starts in September 2027. That does not mean the first-year pay drop is imaginary. You have bills. “Doing something meaningful” is not a payment method accepted by your mortgage provider or landlord.

We would need to look at the actual figures. There is the pension to consider, the holidays, and how the pay goes up, but none of that is a reason to be careless about the first year. And before you accuse me of recruiting you with holidays, yes, they are a benefit. No, every day of them is not spent reclining somewhere while somebody brings me drinks. There is work outside lessons and outside term time. Still, having those breaks matters.

You are also not too old. You are 34, Kelechi. Please behave. A woman in my department started at 41. You would be coming in with experience of working, deadlines, responsibility and dealing with people. You would have plenty to learn, but you would not be starting with nothing.

At our school in Peckham, we have about 1,100 children, and two Year 9 maths groups have had a supply teacher covering them since September. I see how much a steady teacher matters. Someone who knows where the class has got to, notices who is quietly falling behind, and comes back the next day ready to try again. I can imagine you being that person.

That is not me saying you personally have to come and solve the staffing situation. You don’t owe a school your career. But there is a real job here that could use what you are good at.

I was going to write that you are wasting yourself checking other people’s costings. You can hear me saying it, I’m sure. But nine years of your work is not nothing, and I don’t want to dismiss it. What bothers me is hearing you sound so bored by something you spend so much of your life doing. I want you to have a proper look at another possibility before you decide you have to stay.

Applications for next September open soon. Come to Lewisham with me on the 19th. We will listen, ask about the salaried route, the workload, the support and the money. Afterwards we can get something to eat, and you can tell me everything they said that you didn’t believe.

If you come away thinking teaching is not for you, fair enough. I will accept the verdict, although obviously I reserve the right to make one small comment.

Just don’t rule it out from the train on your way back from the same spreadsheet.

Let’s go and find out.

Your guy,

P.S. I paid postage for this. At least check your calendar.
